newsitem.title: USA: Gay marriages legalized in Hawaii in landmark case.
newsitem.headline: Gay marriages legalized in Hawaii in landmark case.

text.p: A judge in Hawaii ruled on Tuesday that same-sex marriages are legal, making the state the first in America to recognise that gay and lesbian couples are entitled to the same privileges as heterosexual married couples.

In his ruling, Judge Kevin Chang found that the Hawaiian state government had failed to establish a "compelling state interest" to justify the prohibition against same-sex marriages, said Dan Foley, a lawyer for three same-sex couples who sued the state in a landmark case.
Foley, jubilant after his meeting with Hawaii Circuit Court Judge Chang to learn of the ruling, told reporters, "I couldn't have gotten more, we got 100 percent."
Hawaii's Deputy Attorney General, Rick Eichor, declined comment.

Foley first filed his suit in 1990 on behalf of the three same-sex couples -- two gay male and one lesbian -- and in 1993 the Hawaiian Supreme Court ordered attorneys for the state to show "compelling" reasons why state discrimination against gay marriages was justified.

One of the plaintiffs in the landmark case, Ninia Baehr, told a news conference in New York after the decision, "People have told us we would never get this far in the courts, but when we heard the news there were tears in my eyes. I thought I would cry if we lost, but we cried for winning."
She and Genora Dancel, both aged 36, hugged each other for a long time after the decision came down "because we thought it would never happen."
The couple were planning a very small wedding on the slopes of Haleakaela, a volcano on the island of Maui.

The case in Hawaii was responsible for a flurry of legislative moves at the national and state level to bar recognition of legalised gay marriages in other states to save states not sanctioning such unions from having to pay benefits afforded to heterosexual married couples.

Earlier this year President Bill Clinton signed into law the "Defense of Marriage" act, prohibiting federal agencies from giving spouses in same-sex marriages the same benefits as those received by heterosexual couples.

According to statistics compiled by the New York-based Lambda Legal Defence and Education Fund, 15 states have passed legislation barring homosexual couples legally married in other states from receiving benefits in their states.

These benefits include Social Security and Medicare, joint insurance for health, home, travel and cars, family leave to take care of a sick partner, hospital visitation rights, the right to will property and money to a partner and the ability to file a joint tax return, among others.
But according to Lambda, 14 mainland states were considering similar legislation to that passed Tuesday in Hawaii, while 17 state legislatures have thrown out anti-gay marriage bills.
